Hydrogenlike Atoms

What you need to know

  • A hydrogenlike atom is one electron bound to a nucleus of charge ZeZeZe: H, He+^++, Li2+^{2+}2+. It is the third model well of the course, after the box and the spring, and the last one the Schrödinger equation solves exactly. The Coulomb attraction −Ze2/4πε0r-Ze^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r−Ze2/4πε0​r has no walls and no bottom; its levels crowd toward E=0E = 0E=0, above which the electron is free.

  • The force is central: VVV depends on rrr alone, so angular momentum is conserved and the angular part of every stationary state is a spherical harmonic YlmY_l^mYlm​ of Lecture 4.4. Only the radial function is new, ψ=Rnl(r) Ylm(θ,ϕ)\psi = R_{nl}(r)\,Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)ψ=Rnl​(r)Ylm​(θ,ϕ), and it solves a one-dimensional Schrödinger equation in an effective potential: the Coulomb attraction plus the centrifugal term l(l+1)ℏ2/2μr2l(l+1)\hbar^2/2\mu r^2l(l+1)ℏ2/2μr2.

  • The constants ℏ\hbarℏ, μ\muμ and e2/4πε0e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0e2/4πε0​ build one length and one energy: the Bohr radius a0=52.9a_0 = 52.9a0​=52.9 pm and the hartree Eh=27.2E_h = 27.2Eh​=27.2 eV. Squeezing the electron into a size aaa costs kinetic energy ℏ2/2μa2\hbar^2/2\mu a^2ℏ2/2μa2 while the attraction pays −e2/4πε0a-e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 a−e2/4πε0​a; the balance at a=a0a = a_0a=a0​ gives −Eh/2=−13.6-E_h/2 = -13.6−Eh​/2=−13.6 eV. That is why the atom does not collapse.

  • The radial function must die at large rrr, and that quantizes the energy: En=−Z2Eh/2n2E_n = -Z^2E_h/2n^2En​=−Z2Eh​/2n2 with n=1,2,3,…n = 1, 2, 3, \dotsn=1,2,3,…, l=0,…,n−1l = 0, \dots, n-1l=0,…,n−1 and m=−l,…,lm = -l, \dots, lm=−l,…,l. The energy depends on nnn alone, so level nnn holds n2n^2n2 states (2n22n^22n2 with spin), a degeneracy special to the 1/r1/r1/r potential. RnlR_{nl}Rnl​ is a polynomial times e−Zr/na0e^{-Zr/na_0}e−Zr/na0​, with n−l−1n - l - 1n−l−1 radial nodes.

  • The level differences give Rydberg’s formula with R∞=Eh/2hc=109 737R_\infty = E_h/2hc = 109\,737R∞​=Eh​/2hc=109737 cm−1^{-1}−1 built from constants, no longer a fit. The reduced mass lowers it slightly for each isotope: deuterium’s lines sit 0.18 nm from hydrogen’s at Hα\alphaα.

A third model well¶

Chapter 4 solved two model systems: a particle between walls and a particle on a spring. The third is an electron attracted to a nucleus. Its potential energy is the Coulomb law, −Ze2/4πε0r-Ze^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r−Ze2/4πε0​r, which has no walls and no spring: it falls without limit as the electron approaches the nucleus and fades to zero far away. The three wells give three patterns of levels:

Source

Fig. The three model wells and their ladders. Box: En∝n2E_n \propto n^2En​∝n2, gaps that grow. Spring: equal gaps ℏω\hbar\omegaℏω. Coulomb: En∝−1/n2E_n \propto -1/n^2En​∝−1/n2, gaps that shrink toward E=0E = 0E=0. Above zero (shaded) the electron is free and any energy is allowed. Each level is drawn across its classically allowed region.

  • The gaps shrink. Each step up the Coulomb ladder is smaller than the last, and the levels pile up against E=0E = 0E=0, the ionization limit. Lecture 1.5 saw this in the hydrogen spectrum: each series of lines converges on a limit, beyond which a continuum begins.

  • Above zero the electron is free. With E>0E > 0E>0 it escapes to infinity, like the free particle of Lecture 3.1: no quantization, any energy. The bound states, E<0E < 0E<0, are the atom.

  • No bottom, but a ground state. The potential falls to −∞-\infty−∞ at the nucleus, yet the lowest level is finite, -13.6 eV. The uncertainty principle sets it, as it set the zero-point energy of the spring (Lecture 4.2); the section on scales shows how.

One electron and one nucleus¶

Two bodies, one reduced mass¶

A hydrogenlike atom has two particles, an electron of mass mem_eme​ and charge −e-e−e and a nucleus of mass mNm_NmN​ and charge +Ze+Ze+Ze. As for the vibrating diatomic of Lecture 4.1, their motion separates into the free flight of the center of mass, which carries no chemistry, and the relative motion of one particle of reduced mass

μ=memNme+mN\mu = \frac{m_em_N}{m_e + m_N}μ=me​+mN​me​mN​​
(1)

at the distance r⃗\vec{r}r of the electron from the nucleus. The nucleus is at least 1836 times heavier than the electron, so μ\muμ differs from mem_eme​ by less than 0.06%: μ=0.99946 me\mu = 0.99946\,m_eμ=0.99946me​ for hydrogen. This lecture writes μ\muμ, and sets μ=me\mu = m_eμ=me​ wherever that precision does not matter. The deuterium example at the end shows where it does.

The Hamiltonian¶

The kinetic energy is that of one particle in three dimensions, as for the box of Lecture 3.2, and the potential energy is the Coulomb attraction:

The hydrogenlike atom
H^=−ℏ22μ∇2−Ze24πε0r,H^ ψ(r,θ,ϕ)=E ψ(r,θ,ϕ)\hat{H} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\nabla^2 - \frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}, \qquad \hat{H}\,\psi(r, \theta, \phi) = E\,\psi(r, \theta, \phi)H^=−2μℏ2​∇2−4πε0​rZe2​,H^ψ(r,θ,ϕ)=Eψ(r,θ,ϕ)
(2)

  • Z=1Z = 1Z=1 for H, 2 for He+^++, 3 for Li2+^{2+}2+: one electron and one nucleus. ε0\varepsilon_0ε0​ is the vacuum permittivity and e=1.602×10−19e = 1.602\times10^{-19}e=1.602×10−19 C

  • Helium, with two electrons, adds a repulsion e2/4πε0r12e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 r_{12}e2/4πε0​r12​ between them, and the equation can no longer be solved exactly (Chapter 7)

A central force¶

Angular momentum is conserved¶

The potential depends on the distance rrr alone, not on the direction. Turn the atom about the nucleus and nothing changes, so by Noether’s theorem (Lecture 4.4) its angular momentum is conserved. In quantum mechanics the same statement is that the Hamiltonian commutes with the angular momentum operators:

[H^,L^2]=0,[H^,L^z]=0[\hat{H}, \hat{L}^2] = 0, \qquad [\hat{H}, \hat{L}_z] = 0[H^,L^2]=0,[H^,L^z​]=0
(3)

The kinetic energy commutes with L^\hat{L}L^ because a turn does not change ∇2\nabla^2∇2, and V(r)V(r)V(r) commutes with it because L^\hat{L}L^ differentiates only with respect to the angles and V(r)V(r)V(r) has none. By Operators 2, commuting operators share eigenfunctions: the stationary states of the atom can be chosen with sharp L2=ℏ2l(l+1)L^2 = \hbar^2l(l+1)L2=ℏ2l(l+1) and Lz=mℏL_z = m\hbarLz​=mℏ. The quantum numbers lll and mmm of Lecture 4.4 label the atom’s states before any new equation is solved.

Separate the angles from the radius¶

Lecture 4.4 split the Laplacian into a radial part and the angular momentum:

∇2=1r2∂∂r(r2∂∂r)−L^2ℏ2r2⟹H^=−ℏ22μ 1r2∂∂r(r2∂∂r)+L^22μr2−Ze24πε0r\nabla^2 = \frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\right) - \frac{\hat{L}^2}{\hbar^2r^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \hat{H} = -\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\,\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{\hat{L}^2}{2\mu r^2} - \frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}∇2=r21​∂r∂​(r2∂r∂​)−ℏ2r2L^2​⟹H^=−2μℏ2​r21​∂r∂​(r2∂r∂​)+2μr2L^2​−4πε0​rZe2​
(4)

The middle term is the rotational kinetic energy L2/2IL^2/2IL2/2I of a particle at distance rrr, with I=μr2I = \mu r^2I=μr2: the rigid rotor of Lecture 4.5, now with a radius that can change. Since L^2\hat{L}^2L^2 acts on the angles alone and everything else on rrr alone, the equation separates:

Write ψ(r,θ,ϕ)=R(r) Ylm(θ,ϕ)\psi(r, \theta, \phi) = R(r)\,Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)ψ(r,θ,ϕ)=R(r)Ylm​(θ,ϕ) and use L^2Ylm=ℏ2l(l+1) Ylm\hat{L}^2Y_l^m = \hbar^2l(l+1)\,Y_l^mL^2Ylm​=ℏ2l(l+1)Ylm​. Every term then carries the same factor YlmY_l^mYlm​, which divides out, leaving an equation in rrr alone:

The radial equation
−ℏ22μ d2udr2+Veff(r) u=E u,Veff(r)=−Ze24πε0r+ℏ2l(l+1)2μr2,u(r)=r R(r),u(0)=0-\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\,\frac{d^2u}{dr^2} + V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r)\,u = E\,u, \qquad V_{\mathrm{eff}}(r) = -\frac{Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r} + \frac{\hbar^2l(l+1)}{2\mu r^2}, \qquad u(r) = r\,R(r), \quad u(0) = 0−2μℏ2​dr2d2u​+Veff​(r)u=Eu,Veff​(r)=−4πε0​rZe2​+2μr2ℏ2l(l+1)​,u(r)=rR(r),u(0)=0

The effective potential¶

The electron moves in the Coulomb attraction plus a repulsive centrifugal term, the rotational kinetic energy L2/2μr2L^2/2\mu r^2L2/2μr2 with L2=ℏ2l(l+1)L^2 = \hbar^2l(l+1)L2=ℏ2l(l+1):

Fig. The effective radial potential for l=0l = 0l=0, 1 and 2, in units of EhE_hEh​ and a0a_0a0​ (defined below). For l=0l = 0l=0 it is the bare Coulomb well. For l>0l > 0l>0 the centrifugal term wins at small rrr and turns the well into a bowl with a bottom at r=l(l+1) a0r = l(l+1)\,a_0r=l(l+1)a0​. Dashed: the levels E1E_1E1​, E2E_2E2​, E3E_3E3​ found below.

  • l=0l = 0l=0: no barrier. The electron can reach the nucleus. Only s states have density at r=0r = 0r=0, which is why they feel the nucleus most strongly (Chapter 7).

  • l>0l > 0l>0: a barrier. The 1/r21/r^21/r2 term beats the 1/r1/r1/r attraction at small rrr and keeps the electron away from the nucleus. The larger lll, the farther out the bowl, so a p electron stays farther from the nucleus than an s electron of the same energy.

  • The level E1E_1E1​ lies below the bowl for l=1l = 1l=1. The l=1l = 1l=1 well bottoms out at −Eh/4-E_h/4−Eh​/4, above E1=−Eh/2E_1 = -E_h/2E1​=−Eh​/2, so no l=1l = 1l=1 state can have the ground-state energy. The lowest level that fits every lll is read off below: n=l+1n = l + 1n=l+1.

One length and one energy¶

H^\hat{H}H^ contains only ℏ\hbarℏ, μ\muμ and the Coulomb strength e2/4πε0e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0e2/4πε0​. As for the oscillator in Lecture 4.2, they build one length and one energy, and the whole solution is written in those units.

Length. Confine the electron within a distance aaa of the nucleus. The uncertainty principle makes its momentum at least about ℏ/a\hbar/aℏ/a, so confinement costs a kinetic energy of order ℏ2/μa2\hbar^2/\mu a^2ℏ2/μa2, while the attraction pays e2/4πε0ae^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 ae2/4πε0​a. The two balance where

ℏ2μa2=e24πε0a⟹a0=4πε0ℏ2μe2=52.9 pm\frac{\hbar^2}{\mu a^2} = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_0 = \frac{4\pi\varepsilon_0\hbar^2}{\mu e^2} = 52.9\ \text{pm}μa2ℏ2​=4πε0​ae2​⟹a0​=μe24πε0​ℏ2​=52.9 pm
(7)

the Bohr radius. Lecture 1.5 found the same length from a circular orbit; here no orbit is assumed, only a size.

Energy. The Coulomb energy at that distance,

Eh=e24πε0a0=ℏ2μa02=4.360×10−18 J=27.21 eVE_h = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 a_0} = \frac{\hbar^2}{\mu a_0^2} = 4.360\times10^{-18}\ \text{J} = 27.21\ \text{eV}Eh​=4πε0​a0​e2​=μa02​ℏ2​=4.360×10−18 J=27.21 eV
(8)

is the hartree. Half of it, 13.6 eV, is the binding energy of the ground state, the Rydberg energy of Lecture 1.5.

The radial equation then reads −12u′′+[−Z/r+l(l+1)/2r2]u=Eu-\frac{1}{2}u'' + \left[-Z/r + l(l+1)/2r^2\right]u = Eu−21​u′′+[−Z/r+l(l+1)/2r2]u=Eu, and the numpy cell below uses it.

Why the atom does not collapse¶

Classically the electron would spiral into the nucleus, radiating as it falls, and the potential offers no floor. Quantum mechanically a state of size aaa has a kinetic energy that grows as the state shrinks. Estimate both parts for a family of trial states ψ=e−r/a\psi = e^{-r/a}ψ=e−r/a of every size:

  1. Kinetic energy from the spread. A state of size aaa has a momentum spread of order ℏ/a\hbar/aℏ/a, so ⟨T⟩=ℏ2/2μa2\langle T\rangle = \hbar^2/2\mu a^2⟨T⟩=ℏ2/2μa2 (exact for this family).

  2. Potential energy from the size. The electron sits at distance about aaa, so ⟨V⟩=−e2/4πε0a\langle V\rangle = -e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 a⟨V⟩=−e2/4πε0​a (also exact for e−r/ae^{-r/a}e−r/a).

  3. Balance. ⟨E⟩=ℏ2/2μa2−e2/4πε0a\langle E\rangle = \hbar^2/2\mu a^2 - e^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0 a⟨E⟩=ℏ2/2μa2−e2/4πε0​a is lowest where d⟨E⟩/da=0d\langle E\rangle/da = 0d⟨E⟩/da=0: at a=a0a = a_0a=a0​, with ⟨E⟩=−Eh/2\langle E\rangle = -E_h/2⟨E⟩=−Eh​/2.

Bottom: the average energy of every size. Squeezing raises the kinetic energy faster than the attraction can pay for it; spreading out gives the attraction away. The lowest total is −Eh/2=−13.6-E_h/2 = -13.6−Eh​/2=−13.6 eV at a=a0a = a_0a=a0​.

  • The trial state (a) has a positive total energy: squeezed to a third of a0a_0a0​ it would not even be bound.

  • The minimum, -13.6 eV, is the exact ground-state energy, because e−r/a0e^{-r/a_0}e−r/a0​ turns out to be the exact ground state (checked below). For any other well this trick gives an upper bound, and Chapter 6 turns it into a method.

Solving the radial equation¶

The tail must die¶

Far from the nucleus Veff→0V_{\mathrm{eff}} \to 0Veff​→0 and the radial equation becomes u′′=κ2uu'' = \kappa^2uu′′=κ2u with κ=−2μE/ℏ\kappa = \sqrt{-2\mu E}/\hbarκ=−2μE​/ℏ for a bound state, E<0E < 0E<0. Its solutions are e−κre^{-\kappa r}e−κr and e+κre^{+\kappa r}e+κr. Near the nucleus the centrifugal term rules and u∝rl+1u \propto r^{l+1}u∝rl+1. Start at u(0)=0u(0) = 0u(0)=0, integrate outward with a trial EEE, and watch the tail: for almost every EEE the growing piece e+κre^{+\kappa r}e+κr survives and uuu blows up. Only at special energies does it die, exactly as for the box and the spring. Try it:

  • Move the slider slowly upward with l=0l = 0l=0. The tail flips from one side to the other each time EEE crosses a level, and the levels appear at −12-\tfrac{1}{2}−21​, −18-\tfrac{1}{8}−81​, −118-\tfrac{1}{18}−181​, −132-\tfrac{1}{32}−321​ hartree: −1/2n2-1/2n^2−1/2n2.

  • Switch to l=1l = 1l=1. The ladder is the same, but its first rung is missing: the lowest l=1l = 1l=1 state sits at −1/8-1/8−1/8, the n=2n = 2n=2 level. With l=2l = 2l=2 the first two are missing. The centrifugal barrier removes the lowest lll rungs, and nnn starts at l+1l + 1l+1.

  • Count the nodes of a bound state: n−l−1n - l - 1n−l−1. Each extra node costs one step up the ladder, as always.

The solution¶

The special energies are found by writing u=rl+1e−κrf(r)u = r^{l+1}e^{-\kappa r}f(r)u=rl+1e−κrf(r) and expanding fff in powers of rrr. The recursion between the coefficients makes the series grow like e+2κre^{+2\kappa r}e+2κr, which would undo the decaying factor, unless the series stops after a finite number of terms, exactly as for the oscillator in Lecture 4.2. It stops only when κa0=Z/n\kappa a_0 = Z/nκa0​=Z/n for a whole number n>ln > ln>l, and that fixes the energy:

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
plt.rcParams.update({"axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False})
cols = {0: TEAL, 1: PURPLE, 2: ORANGE}
R = {(1, 0): lambda p: 2 * np.exp(-p),
     (2, 0): lambda p: (2 - p) * np.exp(-p / 2) / (2 * np.sqrt(2)),
     (2, 1): lambda p: p * np.exp(-p / 2) / (2 * np.sqrt(6)),
     (3, 0): lambda p: 2 * (27 - 18 * p + 2 * p**2) * np.exp(-p / 3) / (81 * np.sqrt(3)),
     (3, 1): lambda p: 4 * (6 - p) * p * np.exp(-p / 3) / (81 * np.sqrt(6)),
     (3, 2): lambda p: 4 * p**2 * np.exp(-p / 3) / (81 * np.sqrt(30))}
nodes = {(1, 0): [], (2, 0): [2.0], (2, 1): [], (3, 0): [1.902, 7.098], (3, 1): [6.0], (3, 2): []}
names = {(1, 0): "1s", (2, 0): "2s", (2, 1): "2p", (3, 0): "3s", (3, 1): "3p", (3, 2): "3d"}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(9.6, 5.0), gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.5, "wspace": 0.22})
for ax, key in zip(axes.flat, [(1, 0), (2, 0), (2, 1), (3, 0), (3, 1), (3, 2)]):
    n, l = key
    xm = 12 if n < 3 else 24
    p = np.linspace(0, xm, 500)
    y = R[key](p)
    ax.axhline(0, color=GRAY, lw=0.8)
    ax.plot(p, y, color=cols[l], lw=2.4)
    ax.plot(nodes[key], [0] * len(nodes[key]), "o", color=CARDINAL, ms=7, zorder=5)
    top = max(y.max(), 0.08) if n > 1 else y.max()
    ax.set_xlim(0, xm); ax.set_ylim(min(-0.22 * top, 1.15 * y.min()), 1.15 * top)
    ax.set_title(names[key], fontsize=13.5, color=cols[l], weight="bold")
    ax.tick_params(labelsize=10)
for ax in axes[1]:
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$r$ ($a_0$)", fontsize=11.5)

The same equation on a grid¶

The radial equation is the one-dimensional equation that Lecture 3.5 turned into a matrix: sample uuu on a grid of spacing Δr\Delta rΔr, write −12u′′-\frac{1}{2}u''−21​u′′ with the three-point formula, add VeffV_{\mathrm{eff}}Veff​ on the diagonal, and diagonalize. The wall at the nucleus is u(0)=0u(0) = 0u(0)=0, so the grid starts just past r=0r = 0r=0. In atomic units, for Z=1Z = 1Z=1:

import numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import eigh_tridiagonal

dr = 0.01                                        # grid spacing, units of a0
r = np.arange(dr, 80, dr)                        # r > 0: the wall u(0) = 0 sits at the nucleus
for l in (0, 1, 2):
    V = -1 / r + l * (l + 1) / (2 * r**2)        # V_eff in hartree, Z = 1
    diag, off = 1 / dr**2 + V, -np.ones(len(r) - 1) / (2 * dr**2)
    E = eigh_tridiagonal(diag, off, select="i", select_range=(0, 2))[0]
    print(f"l = {l}:", np.round(E, 4))
l = 0: [-0.5    -0.125  -0.0556]
l = 1: [-0.125  -0.0556 -0.0313]
l = 2: [-0.0556 -0.0313 -0.02  ]

  • Each row of the matrix holds three numbers (the point and its two neighbors), so eigh_tridiagonal does what eigh did in Lecture 3.5, only faster on 8000 points.

  • The l=0l = 0l=0 column reads −12,−18,−118-\tfrac{1}{2}, -\tfrac{1}{8}, -\tfrac{1}{18}−21​,−81​,−181​: the levels n=1,2,3n = 1, 2, 3n=1,2,3. The l=1l = 1l=1 column starts at −18-\tfrac{1}{8}−81​ and l=2l = 2l=2 at −118-\tfrac{1}{18}−181​: the first level of each lll is n=l+1n = l + 1n=l+1.

  • The same energies appear in every column where they are allowed. The grid knows nothing about the formula −1/2n2-1/2n^2−1/2n2; the degeneracy in lll comes out of the Coulomb potential by itself.

Energy levels and degeneracy¶

Fig. The levels of hydrogen up to n=4n = 4n=4, one bar for each state (l,m)(l, m)(l,m). All states of a given nnn share one energy, so level nnn holds 1+3+5+⋯=n21 + 3 + 5 + \dots = n^21+3+5+⋯=n2 states. Above zero (shaded) the electron is free.

  • n2n^2n2 states per level. For each lll from 0 to n−1n - 1n−1 there are 2l+12l + 12l+1 values of mmm, and ∑l=0n−1(2l+1)=n2\sum_{l=0}^{n-1}(2l+1) = n^2∑l=0n−1​(2l+1)=n2. The electron’s spin (Lecture 5.3) doubles it: 2n22n^22n2, the lengths of the rows of the periodic table, 2, 8, 18, 32.

  • The mmm degeneracy is rotational symmetry. States that differ only in mmm are the same state pointed in different directions, as for the rigid rotor. A magnetic field, which picks out a direction, splits them (Lecture 5.3).

  • The lll degeneracy is special to 1/r1/r1/r. Nothing about rotational symmetry requires 2s and 2p to share an energy; they do in hydrogen because of a further symmetry of the Coulomb potential alone, the same one that keeps planetary orbits from precessing. In atoms with more than one electron the inner electrons screen the nucleus, the potential is no longer 1/r1/r1/r, and 2s drops below 2p, 3s below 3p below 3d (Chapter 7). The effective potential shows why: s electrons penetrate to the nucleus, where the screening is weakest.

Example: the states with n=3n = 3n=3

List the states of hydrogen with n=3n = 3n=3 and what a measurement of EEE, L2L^2L2 and LzL_zLz​ gives in each.

  • l=0l = 0l=0: 3s, one state (m=0m = 0m=0). l=1l = 1l=1: 3p, three states (m=−1,0,1m = -1, 0, 1m=−1,0,1). l=2l = 2l=2: 3d, five states (m=−2,…,2m = -2, \dots, 2m=−2,…,2). Nine in all, 32, and 18 with spin.

  • Every one has E3=−13.6/9=−1.51E_3 = -13.6/9 = -1.51E3​=−13.6/9=−1.51 eV. L2L^2L2 is 0, 2ℏ22\hbar^22ℏ2 or 6ℏ26\hbar^26ℏ2 for s, p, d, and Lz=mℏL_z = m\hbarLz​=mℏ.

  • Each has n−1=2n - 1 = 2n−1=2 nodes: 3s has two radial nodes, 3p one radial and one angular, 3d two angular.

Hydrogenlike ions¶

Everything scales with the nuclear charge. The length a0/Za_0/Za0​/Z and the energy Z2EhZ^2E_hZ2Eh​ come straight out of the ground-state check above: a larger nucleus pulls the electron in by 1/Z1/Z1/Z and binds it Z2Z^2Z2 times more tightly.

Example: He+^++ and Li2+^{2+}2+

Find the ionization energy, the size of the ground state and the wavelength of the 2→12 \to 12→1 line for He+^++ and Li2+^{2+}2+.

  • Ionization energy, −E1=13.6 Z2-E_1 = 13.6\,Z^2−E1​=13.6Z2 eV: 54.4 eV for He+^++ and 122.4 eV for Li2+^{2+}2+ (hydrogen: 13.6 eV).

  • Size, a0/Za_0/Za0​/Z: 26.5 pm and 17.6 pm.

  • The 2→12 \to 12→1 photon carries 34⋅13.6 Z2\frac{3}{4}\cdot13.6\,Z^243​⋅13.6Z2 eV: 40.8 eV, λ=30.4\lambda = 30.4λ=30.4 nm for He+^++ and 91.8 eV, 13.5 nm for Li2+^{2+}2+, against 121.6 nm for hydrogen. All in the extreme ultraviolet; the stripped ions exist in stellar atmospheres and plasmas.

The spectrum¶

An atom absorbs or emits a photon when it jumps between two levels, hν=En2−En1h\nu = E_{n_2} - E_{n_1}hν=En2​​−En1​​. In wavenumbers, ν~=ΔE/hc\tilde{\nu} = \Delta E/hcν~=ΔE/hc:

Spectral lines of a hydrogenlike atom
ν~=R Z2(1n12−1n22),R∞=Eh2hc=mee48ε02h3c=109 737 cm−1\tilde{\nu} = R\,Z^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right), \qquad R_\infty = \frac{E_h}{2hc} = \frac{m_ee^4}{8\varepsilon_0^2h^3c} = 109\,737\ \text{cm}^{-1}ν~=RZ2(n12​1​−n22​1​),R∞​=2hcEh​​=8ε02​h3cme​e4​=109737 cm−1
(15)
RM=R∞1+me/mNfor a nucleus of mass mN:RH=109 678 cm−1R_M = \frac{R_\infty}{1 + m_e/m_N} \qquad\text{for a nucleus of mass } m_N: \quad R_H = 109\,678\ \text{cm}^{-1}RM​=1+me​/mN​R∞​​for a nucleus of mass mN​:RH​=109678 cm−1
(16)

  • Rydberg’s formula of Lecture 1.5, with the constant now built from mem_eme​, eee, ε0\varepsilon_0ε0​, hhh and ccc. R∞R_\inftyR∞​ is the value for an infinitely heavy nucleus; the reduced mass μ=me/(1+me/mN)\mu = m_e/(1 + m_e/m_N)μ=me​/(1+me​/mN​) lowers it for a real one

  • n1=1n_1 = 1n1​=1: the Lyman series (ultraviolet); n1=2n_1 = 2n1​=2: Balmer (visible); n1=3n_1 = 3n1​=3: Paschen (infrared). Each series ends at its limit RZ2/n12RZ^2/n_1^2RZ2/n12​, beyond which the electron is free and the spectrum is continuous

# synced: balmer_lines
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.animation import FuncAnimation
from IPython.display import HTML

TEAL, CARDINAL, GRAY, PURPLE, ORANGE = "#107895", "#C8102E", "#6c757d", "#6a3d9a", "#e07b00"
RH, RD = 109677.58, 109707.43                                    # Rydberg constants of H and D, cm^-1
lam = lambda R, n: 1e7 / (R * (0.25 - 1 / n**2))                 # Balmer wavelength in nm, vacuum
w = np.linspace(355, 700, 1381)                                  # colour of each wavelength, a piecewise rainbow
Rc = np.where(w < 440, (440 - w) / 60, np.where(w < 510, 0, np.where(w < 580, (w - 510) / 70, 1)))
Gc = np.where(w < 440, 0, np.where(w < 490, (w - 440) / 50, np.where(w < 580, 1, np.where(w < 645, (645 - w) / 65, 0))))
Bc = np.where(w < 490, 1, np.where(w < 510, (510 - w) / 20, 0))
fade = np.clip(np.where(w < 420, 0.3 + 0.7 * (w - 380) / 40, np.where(w > 650, 0.35 + 0.65 * (700 - w) / 50, 1)), 0, 1)
rgb = np.clip(np.stack([Rc, Gc, Bc], -1) * fade[:, None], 0, 1)
colour_at = lambda x: rgb[np.argmin(np.abs(w - x))]
fig, (ax, bx) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(9.6, 4.6), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1.15, 1], "hspace": 0.75})
for a_ in (ax, bx):
    a_.set_facecolor("#111111"); a_.set_yticks([])
    for sp in a_.spines.values():
        sp.set_color("#444444")
    a_.tick_params(labelsize=10.5)
ax.imshow((0.22 * rgb)[None, :, :], extent=[355, 700, 0, 1], aspect="auto", zorder=0)
for n in range(3, 11):
    x = lam(RH, n)
    ax.vlines(x, 0, 1, color=colour_at(x), lw=2.6 if n < 7 else 1.4, zorder=2)
    if n <= 6:
        ax.text(x, 1.06, rf"$n = {n}$", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11)
xl = lam(RH, 1e9)
ax.vlines(xl, 0, 1, color="#cccccc", lw=1.4, ls="--", zorder=2)
ax.text(xl, 1.06, "limit", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11, color=GRAY)
ax.set_xlim(355, 700); ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.set_xlabel("wavelength (nm)", fontsize=11.5)
xH, xD = lam(RH, 3), lam(RD, 3)
for x, name in ((xH, "H"), (xD, "D")):
    bx.vlines(x, 0, 1, color=colour_at(656.4), lw=3, zorder=2)
    bx.text(x, 1.06, name, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=12.5)
bx.annotate("", xy=(xD, 0.5), xytext=(xH, 0.5), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="<->", color="white", lw=1.2, shrinkA=3, shrinkB=3))
bx.text(0.5 * (xH + xD), 0.57, f"{xH - xD:.2f} nm", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=11, color="white")
bx.set_xlim(655.9, 656.85); bx.set_ylim(0, 1)
bx.set_xticks([656.0, 656.2, 656.4, 656.6, 656.8])
bx.set_xlabel(r"wavelength (nm), near $n = 3 \to 2$", fontsize=11.5)
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.03, right=0.98, top=0.9, bottom=0.12)
plt.show()

Fig. Top: the Balmer series of hydrogen as a spectroscope shows it, lines from n=3,4,5,…n = 3, 4, 5, \dotsn=3,4,5,… down to n=2n = 2n=2 crowding toward the series limit at 364.7 nm. Bottom: the red Hα\alphaα line at high resolution. Deuterium’s line lies 0.18 nm to the blue of hydrogen’s, because its heavier nucleus gives a slightly larger reduced mass.

Lecture 1.5 reached the same levels with Bohr’s orbits. The Schrödinger equation keeps the levels and discards the orbit: the ground state has l=0l = 0l=0, no angular momentum at all, and the electron is a standing wave e−r/a0e^{-r/a_0}e−r/a0​ that is densest at the nucleus. Where Bohr’s model stops, at helium, intensities and fine structure, the wave equation continues.

Example: deuterium

Hydrogen’s Hα\alphaα line (3→23 \to 23→2) is at 656.47 nm in vacuum (656.28 nm in air). Where is deuterium’s? (mp=1836.15 mem_p = 1836.15\,m_emp​=1836.15me​, md=3670.48 mem_d = 3670.48\,m_emd​=3670.48me​.)

The two atoms have the same ZZZ and the same formula; only the reduced mass differs, and ν~∝RM∝μ\tilde{\nu} \propto R_M \propto \muν~∝RM​∝μ:

μHme=11+1/1836.15=0.999456,μDme=11+1/3670.48=0.999728\frac{\mu_H}{m_e} = \frac{1}{1 + 1/1836.15} = 0.999456, \qquad \frac{\mu_D}{m_e} = \frac{1}{1 + 1/3670.48} = 0.999728me​μH​​=1+1/1836.151​=0.999456,me​μD​​=1+1/3670.481​=0.999728
(17)
λD=λH μHμD=656.47 nm×0.9994560.999728=656.29 nm\lambda_D = \lambda_H\,\frac{\mu_H}{\mu_D} = 656.47\ \text{nm}\times\frac{0.999456}{0.999728} = 656.29\ \text{nm}λD​=λH​μD​μH​​=656.47 nm×0.9997280.999456​=656.29 nm
(18)

The shift, 0.18 nm, is how Urey found deuterium in 1931 (Nobel Prize 1934): a faint satellite on the blue side of every Balmer line. The lines of ordinary hydrogen sit at RH=109 678R_H = 109\,678RH​=109678 cm−1^{-1}−1, not R∞=109 737R_\infty = 109\,737R∞​=109737: the nucleus moves too.

Going further: radial averages

Averages of powers of rrr in the state ψnlm\psi_{nlm}ψnlm​, ⟨rk⟩=∫0∞rk Rnl2 r2 dr\langle r^k\rangle = \int_0^\infty r^k\,R_{nl}^2\,r^2\,dr⟨rk⟩=∫0∞​rkRnl2​r2dr, come out in closed form:

⟨r⟩=a0n2Z[1+12(1−l(l+1)n2)],⟨r2⟩=a02n4Z2[1+32(1−l(l+1)−1/3n2)]\langle r\rangle = \frac{a_0n^2}{Z}\left[1 + \frac{1}{2}\left(1 - \frac{l(l+1)}{n^2}\right)\right], \qquad \langle r^2\rangle = \frac{a_0^2n^4}{Z^2}\left[1 + \frac{3}{2}\left(1 - \frac{l(l+1) - 1/3}{n^2}\right)\right]⟨r⟩=Za0​n2​[1+21​(1−n2l(l+1)​)],⟨r2⟩=Z2a02​n4​[1+23​(1−n2l(l+1)−1/3​)]
(19)
⟨1r⟩=Za0n2,⟨1r2⟩=Z2a02n3(l+1/2),⟨1r3⟩=Z3a03n3 l (l+1/2)(l+1)\left\langle\frac{1}{r}\right\rangle = \frac{Z}{a_0n^2}, \qquad \left\langle\frac{1}{r^2}\right\rangle = \frac{Z^2}{a_0^2n^3(l + 1/2)}, \qquad \left\langle\frac{1}{r^3}\right\rangle = \frac{Z^3}{a_0^3n^3\,l\,(l + 1/2)(l + 1)}⟨r1​⟩=a0​n2Z​,⟨r21​⟩=a02​n3(l+1/2)Z2​,⟨r31​⟩=a03​n3l(l+1/2)(l+1)Z3​
(20)

  • ⟨r⟩\langle r\rangle⟨r⟩ grows as n2n^2n2: the size of the state. ⟨1/r⟩\langle 1/r\rangle⟨1/r⟩ gives the average potential energy, ⟨V⟩=−Z2Eh/n2=2En\langle V\rangle = -Z^2E_h/n^2 = 2E_n⟨V⟩=−Z2Eh​/n2=2En​, so the average kinetic energy is −En-E_n−En​: the virial theorem of the Coulomb problem

  • ⟨1/r3⟩\langle 1/r^3\rangle⟨1/r3⟩ enters the spin-orbit coupling of Lecture 5.3

What the solution gives, and what it leaves¶

The hydrogen atom is solved: every level, every state. Three lectures build on it.

  • Shapes and sizes. ∣ψnlm∣2|\psi_{nlm}|^2∣ψnlm​∣2 and the radial distribution r2Rnl2r^2R_{nl}^2r2Rnl2​, the real orbitals pxp_xpx​, pyp_ypy​, dxyd_{xy}dxy​, most probable and average distances: Atomic Orbitals.

  • Spin. The electron carries its own angular momentum, s=12s = \frac{1}{2}s=21​, which the Schrödinger equation does not contain. It doubles every level, couples to the orbital motion (fine structure, a 10-4 eV splitting of the levels) and responds to magnetic fields: Lecture 5.3.

  • More electrons. Helium’s two electrons repel each other and the exact solution is gone, but the hydrogen orbitals remain the language: Chapter 7 builds atoms from them, with the lll degeneracy lifted by screening, and Chapter 8 builds molecules.

Problems¶

Problem 1: Positronium¶

An electron and a positron (its antiparticle: the same mass, the opposite charge) can bind into positronium, which lives about 10-7 s before annihilating. Find its reduced mass, its ground-state energy, the size of its ground state, and the wavelength of its 2→12 \to 12→1 line.

Solution

With two equal masses, μ=meme/(me+me)=me/2\mu = m_em_e/(m_e + m_e) = m_e/2μ=me​me​/(me​+me​)=me​/2. Every energy of a hydrogenlike system is proportional to μ\muμ and every length inversely proportional to it (a0∝1/μa_0 \propto 1/\mua0​∝1/μ, Eh∝μE_h \propto \muEh​∝μ), with Z=1Z = 1Z=1:

  • E1=−13.6 eV×12=−6.80E_1 = -13.6\ \text{eV}\times\tfrac{1}{2} = -6.80E1​=−13.6 eV×21​=−6.80 eV; the levels are −6.80/n2-6.80/n^2−6.80/n2 eV.

  • Size: 2a0=1062a_0 = 1062a0​=106 pm, twice hydrogen’s.

  • The 2→12 \to 12→1 photon: 34×6.80=5.10\tfrac{3}{4}\times6.80 = 5.1043​×6.80=5.10 eV, λ=1240 eV nm/5.10 eV=243\lambda = 1240\ \text{eV nm}/5.10\ \text{eV} = 243λ=1240 eV nm/5.10 eV=243 nm, twice the Lyman α\alphaα wavelength of hydrogen (121.6 nm). Measured: 243.0 nm.

Positronium is the cleanest test of the reduced mass: nothing in it is heavy.

Problem 2: Muonic hydrogen¶

A muon is a heavy electron, mμ=206.8 mem_\mu = 206.8\,m_emμ​=206.8me​, and a proton can capture one. Find the reduced mass of muonic hydrogen, the size of its ground state, its ground-state energy in keV, and the energy of its 2→12 \to 12→1 photon. The proton has a radius of 0.84 fm; compare it with the size of the state, and explain why the levels of muonic hydrogen are used to measure the size of the proton.

Problem 3: Check the 2p state¶

Show that u(r)=r2e−r/2au(r) = r^2e^{-r/2a}u(r)=r2e−r/2a solves the radial equation with l=1l = 1l=1, using atomic units (ℏ=μ=e=4πε0=1\hbar = \mu = e = 4\pi\varepsilon_0 = 1ℏ=μ=e=4πε0​=1, Z=1Z = 1Z=1), and find aaa and EEE.

Solution

With l=1l = 1l=1 the centrifugal term is l(l+1)/2r2=1/r2l(l+1)/2r^2 = 1/r^2l(l+1)/2r2=1/r2, and the equation is −12u′′+(−1r+1r2)u=Eu-\frac{1}{2}u'' + \left(-\frac{1}{r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\right)u = Eu−21​u′′+(−r1​+r21​)u=Eu. Differentiate:

u′=(2r−r22a)e−r/2a,u′′=(2−2ra+r24a2)e−r/2au' = \left(2r - \frac{r^2}{2a}\right)e^{-r/2a}, \qquad u'' = \left(2 - \frac{2r}{a} + \frac{r^2}{4a^2}\right)e^{-r/2a}u′=(2r−2ar2​)e−r/2a,u′′=(2−a2r​+4a2r2​)e−r/2a
(21)

Insert and divide by e−r/2ae^{-r/2a}e−r/2a:

−1+ra−r28a2−r+1=E r2-1 + \frac{r}{a} - \frac{r^2}{8a^2} - r + 1 = E\,r^2−1+ar​−8a2r2​−r+1=Er2
(22)

The constants cancel on their own (−12⋅2-\frac{1}{2}\cdot2−21​⋅2 against 1r2⋅r2\frac{1}{r^2}\cdot r^2r21​⋅r2). The terms linear in rrr cancel only if a=1a = 1a=1, that is a=a0a = a_0a=a0​, and what remains is −r2/8=Er2-r^2/8 = Er^2−r2/8=Er2: E=−18E = -\frac{1}{8}E=−81​ hartree =−3.40= -3.40=−3.40 eV, the n=2n = 2n=2 level. So R21∝re−r/2a0R_{21} \propto re^{-r/2a_0}R21​∝re−r/2a0​, as in the table, with no radial node, and the l=1l = 1l=1 ladder starts at n=2n = 2n=2.

Problem 4: The n=4n = 4n=4 shell¶

List every state of hydrogen with n=4n = 4n=4 by its letters and mmm values, and check that they number n2n^2n2. For each lll, give the number of radial nodes, the number of angular nodes, and whether the state has any density at the nucleus. Which of these states would you expect to lie lowest in a sodium atom, where the inner electrons screen the nucleus, and why?

Problem 5: A Rydberg atom¶

Hydrogen can be prepared in the level n=100n = 100n=100. Estimate the size of this state, and find the frequency and wavelength of the photon emitted in the transition 100→99100 \to 99100→99. Compare it with the approximation ΔE≈2⋅Eh2/n3\Delta E \approx 2\cdot\frac{E_h}{2}/n^3ΔE≈2⋅2Eh​​/n3 obtained by differentiating EnE_nEn​.

Solution

  • Size: n2a0=104×52.9 pm=0.53 μmn^2a_0 = 10^4\times52.9\ \text{pm} = 0.53\ \mu\text{m}n2a0​=104×52.9 pm=0.53 μm, larger than a small virus. Such Rydberg atoms are so big and so loosely bound (E100=−1.36E_{100} = -1.36E100​=−1.36 meV) that a stray electric field tears them apart.

  • The photon: ΔE=13.606 eV(1992−11002)=13.606 eV×2.030×10−6=2.762×10−5\Delta E = 13.606\ \text{eV}\left(\frac{1}{99^2} - \frac{1}{100^2}\right) = 13.606\ \text{eV}\times2.030\times10^{-6} = 2.762\times10^{-5}ΔE=13.606 eV(9921​−10021​)=13.606 eV×2.030×10−6=2.762×10−5 eV, so ν=ΔE/h=6.68\nu = \Delta E/h = 6.68ν=ΔE/h=6.68 GHz and λ=4.49\lambda = 4.49λ=4.49 cm: a radio wave.

  • The derivative estimate, dEn/dn=Eh/n3=27.2 eV/106=2.72×10−5dE_n/dn = E_h/n^3 = 27.2\ \text{eV}/10^6 = 2.72\times10^{-5}dEn​/dn=Eh​/n3=27.2 eV/106=2.72×10−5 eV, is 1.5% low, because the gap is not quite the slope at n=100n = 100n=100.

Radio astronomers observe these lines from hydrogen between the stars (n=110→109n = 110 \to 109n=110→109 at 5.0 GHz, for instance), and the frequency Eh/hn3E_h/hn^3Eh​/hn3 is the classical orbital frequency of Bohr’s model at that radius: at large nnn the quantum atom radiates at the frequency a classical orbit would, the correspondence principle again.

Problem 6: Ionizing hydrogen with light¶

A hydrogen atom in its ground state absorbs a photon of 15.0 eV. What happens, and how fast does the electron leave? What happens instead if the photon carries 10.0 eV?

Solution

  • 15.0 eV exceeds the ionization energy, 13.6 eV, so the electron is freed with the remainder: 12mev2=1.4\frac{1}{2}m_ev^2 = 1.421​me​v2=1.4 eV, v=2×1.4 eV/me=7.0×105v = \sqrt{2\times1.4\ \text{eV}/m_e} = 7.0\times10^5v=2×1.4 eV/me​​=7.0×105 m/s. Above the series limit any photon energy works, because the free electron can take any energy: the photoelectric effect of Lecture 1.3, with the atom as the metal.

  • 10.0 eV matches no level difference from n=1n = 1n=1 (the smallest is E2−E1=10.2E_2 - E_1 = 10.2E2​−E1​=10.2 eV), and it cannot ionize. The atom is transparent to it. Below the ionization limit the atom absorbs only at its lines; above it, everywhere.

Problem 8: Bohr’s orbit and the real ground state¶

Bohr’s ground state (Lecture 1.5) is a circular orbit of radius a0a_0a0​ with angular momentum L=ℏL = \hbarL=ℏ. The Schrödinger ground state has l=0l = 0l=0, no angular momentum, and the same energy. (a) Is there any state of hydrogen with energy E1E_1E1​ and L=ℏL = \hbarL=ℏ? Use the effective potential for l=1l = 1l=1 to answer. (b) Bohr’s orbits have L=nℏL = n\hbarL=nℏ. What values of LLL does the quantum atom actually allow in the level nnn? (c) In what sense does a0a_0a0​ still describe the quantum ground state, if the electron is not on a circle?
